title: Transit use by home location: a two-way table

stimulus.title: Home location and weekly transit use
stimulus.html:
A regional transit agency surveyed a random sample of 500 adults in a metro area. Each adult reported where they live and whether they use public transit at least once a week. The results are in the table (invented data).
Home location and weekly transit use for 500 adults
Home locationUses transit weeklyDoes notTotal
Downtown9664160
Inner suburbs84116200
Outer suburbs28112140
Total208292500

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: An adult is selected at random from the 500 in the sample. (i) Calculate the probability that the adult uses transit weekly, given that the adult lives downtown. (ii) Calculate the probability that the adult lives downtown, given that the adult uses transit weekly. (iii) Explain why the two probabilities are different.

rubric.point: (i) P(uses transit | downtown) = 96/160 = 0.6, with the work shown.
(ii) P(downtown | uses transit) = 96/208, about 0.462, with the work shown.
(iii) Explains that the conditions (and so the denominators) differ: (i) is a share of the 160 downtown adults, (ii) is a share of the 208 transit users.
accept: The first divides by the number who live downtown, the second by the number who use transit
The groups being described are different

parts.sample: (i) P(transit | downtown) = 96/160 = 0.6. (ii) P(downtown | transit) = 96/208 = 0.462. (iii) Both use the 96 downtown adults who ride transit, but (i) is the share of the 160 downtown adults who ride transit, while (ii) is the share of the 208 weekly transit users who live downtown. The groups we condition on are different sizes, so the probabilities differ.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Describe the association between home location and weekly transit use for the adults in the sample. Support your answer with appropriate calculations.

rubric.point: Calculates the conditional proportion who use transit weekly for each location: downtown 0.60, inner suburbs 0.42, outer suburbs 0.20.
accept: The three conditional proportions of non-users (0.40, 0.58, 0.80) also earn the point

rubric.point: Describes the association in context with a comparison: the farther from downtown adults live, the smaller the proportion who use transit weekly, so location and transit use are associated.
accept: Downtown adults are most likely and outer-suburb adults least likely to use transit weekly
A statement that compares counts (96, 84, 28) rather than proportions does not earn the point

parts.sample: The proportion who use transit weekly is 96/160 = 0.60 downtown, 84/200 = 0.42 in the inner suburbs, and 28/140 = 0.20 in the outer suburbs. In this sample, home location and transit use are associated: the farther from downtown adults live, the smaller the proportion who use transit weekly.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: For an adult selected at random from the sample, are the events "lives downtown" and "uses transit weekly" independent? Justify your answer.

rubric.point: Compares a conditional probability with the matching unconditional one (or the joint probability with a product): P(transit | downtown) = 0.6 and P(transit) = 208/500 = 0.416.
Concludes the events are not independent because the probabilities differ (knowing the adult lives downtown changes the probability of weekly transit use).
accept: Not independent, since 0.6 is not equal to 0.416
A conclusion that the events are not independent because they "overlap" or because 96 is not 0 does not earn the point

parts.sample: P(transit) = 208/500 = 0.416, but P(transit | downtown) = 96/160 = 0.6. Because these are not equal, knowing that the adult lives downtown changes the probability that the adult uses transit weekly, so the events are not independent.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Calculate the probability that a randomly selected adult from the sample lives downtown or uses transit weekly.

rubric.point: Uses the general addition rule (or a correct count) to get 160/500 + 208/500 − 96/500 = 272/500 = 0.544.
accept: 1 minus the 228 adults who neither live downtown nor ride transit, 1 - 228/500 = 0.544

parts.sample: P(downtown or transit) = P(downtown) + P(transit) - P(downtown and transit) = 160/500 + 208/500 - 96/500 = 272/500 = 0.544.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: A city council member claims that adults who live downtown are more than twice as likely to use transit weekly as adults who live in the outer suburbs. Do the data support the claim? Justify your answer.

rubric.point: Compares the two conditional proportions correctly: 0.60 for downtown and 0.20 for outer suburbs, so downtown adults in the sample are 3 times as likely to use transit weekly.

States a conclusion in context that the sample supports the claim, and notes that because the sample was random, the pattern can be generalized to adults in the metro area (allowing that another sample would give somewhat different proportions).
accept: Yes, in this random sample downtown adults use transit at three times the rate of outer-suburb adults, so the data support the claim for the metro area
A conclusion based on the counts 96 and 28 does not earn the point

parts.sample: Yes. In the sample, 96/160 = 0.60 of downtown adults use transit weekly, compared with 28/140 = 0.20 of outer-suburb adults. Since 0.60 is three times 0.20, downtown adults in the sample are more than twice as likely to use transit weekly. Because the 500 adults were a random sample from the metro area, the data support the council member's claim for the metro area, although a different random sample would give somewhat different proportions.
